system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Draft (SPA-003 and Disclosure Letter)

## Bottom line

The Seller's package shifts almost all known risk to the Buyer and then limits what the Buyer can recover on everything else. The main problems are:

1. **Known issues are unpriced and unprotected.** The Riverlark debt, Bluefen consent, Ironquay IP, employee bonuses, supplier commitments and the privacy incident are disclosed, but no price, indemnity or condition covers them.
2. **Disclosure and the buyer-knowledge clause together remove most warranty recovery.** Clause 1.1 discloses the entire data room, and clause 8.3 bars claims for anything the Buyer "had knowledge of" or could have "discovered."
3. **Recovery limits are weak even before those carve-outs.** The cap, deductible basket and time limits are all seller-favourable, and title and capacity are pulled into the same limits.

I have worked from the Seller's summary and disclosure letter, not the full SPA. Clause cross-references in the summary (for example 9.3, 12.8, 20.5, 2/7, 3/6.3) need checking against the full draft before any mark-up.

## Preliminary points on the Seller's framing

- **"FINAL / not to be re-opened."** This is a negotiating position, not a legal constraint. Unless the principal-level agreement is documented and we have seen it, the Buyer is not bound by it. We should ask for the written record of any agreed terms.
- **"Market" figures** (10–20% caps, ~1% baskets, 12–18 month limitation periods). These are the Seller's assertions. Market terms vary with deal structure, risk profile and whether W&I insurance is used. Our figures should come from our own adviser's precedent and insurance broker input, not from the Seller's preamble.
- **Seller's own disclosures undercut the "fair and balanced" claim.** The disclosure letter itself lists material unresolved items (Section 2 to 10). Under the Seller's structure, the Buyer would carry every one of them.

## Issue-by-issue analysis

### A. Recovery limits (clauses 12.1, 12.2)

| Term | Seller position | Problem for Buyer | Opening ask | Fallback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| General cap | 20% of price (AUD 4.8m) | Known quantified exposures (~AUD 4.13m, see Part B) would consume almost the whole cap | 30% (AUD 7.2m) | 20%, only if known items sit outside the cap |
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | Excludes many small but related claims; a single claim threshold is aggressive | AUD 10,000 (or no de minimis for related claims) | AUD 15,000 |
| Basket | AUD 250,000 (~1.04%), deductible ("excess only") | The Buyer absorbs the first AUD 250k of every claim across the warranty set | Tipping basket (first-dollar recovery once exceeded) at ~0.5% (AUD 120,000) | Tipping basket at 1% |
| Fundamental / title / capacity | Same cap and time limits as general | Title to shares is the core asset. Capping it at 20% of price is unacceptable | Up to 100% of price, no de minimis or basket, 6-year period | Up to 100% of price, no de minimis or basket, longer period |

Points to note:
- A deductible basket sits badly with a cap set as a percentage of price. Combined, they mean the Buyer recovers only on losses well above the threshold.
- Clause 12.2 says "only the excess above the basket is recoverable." That is a deductible structure and should be struck.

### B. Known exposures (should not sit inside the general cap)

Quantifiable items from the disclosure letter:

| Item | Amount (AUD) | Seller position | Buyer ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility (DD-003) | ~3,200,000 | Release "following Completion" | Repay at Completion from the price, with payoff letter and discharge of all security (including PPSR) as a completion deliverable |
| Employee bonuses (DD-005) | 420,000 plus on-costs (payroll tax, superannuation and any other employer costs, unquantified) | Not in funds flow; Seller says "a matter for the Seller" | Treat as a debt-like item deducted from price, or paid by Seller through payroll before/at Completion; include on-costs in the calculation |
| Ironquay SOW3 (DD-004, DD-010) | 180,000 open | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment, "adequate" | Seller pays all open SOW fees before Completion, or a price deduction; receipt and confirmatory assignment as a condition; full indemnity for Ironquay IP title and third-party claims |
| Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008, DD-011) | 330,000 aggregate | "Ordinary course" | Confirm terms and termination rights; treat any unavoidable commitment as a debt-like item or price adjustment; covenant against new commitments outside the ordinary course without Buyer consent |
| **Subtotal (quantified)** | **~4,130,000** | | Plus unquantified items below |

Unquantified exposures:
- **Bluefen (DD-002).** Roughly AUD 3.6m, or ~30% of FY26 revenue, is at risk if the change-control consent is not obtained. Clauses 3 and 6.3 use "reasonable endeavours" and treat consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. This must be a condition precedent that the Buyer can waive, with no deemed satisfaction. If Bluefen terminates or imposes adverse conditions after Completion, the Buyer needs a specific indemnity or price mechanism (for example, an escrow or deferred consideration tied to Bluefen revenue for 12 to 24 months).
- **Privacy incident (DD-006).** Around 1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) may have been sent to an unintended external address. Paperbark's revenue (implied roughly AUD 12m from the Bluefen percentage) suggests it is likely an APP entity under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). If the incident is an eligible data breach under the NDB scheme (Part IIIC), notification obligations and regulator exposure follow. The Seller's position that it is "not expected to be material" is not supported by the disclosure, which says the investigation is preliminary and the scope and access questions are open. The Buyer needs: a completed forensic/investigation report before signing or as a condition; a specific indemnity (outside the general cap, with its own cap and a longer period) covering notification, regulator, remediation and third-party claim costs; and a Seller warranty on prior incidents.
- **Office lease (DD-007).** Confirm whether landlord consent is required for the share sale. If so, make it a condition or obtain a landlord estoppel and consent before Completion.
- **Mossvale (DD-009).** The Seller says the assignment restriction does not bite on a share sale. Ask for a written confirmation or a short legal analysis, and a warranty plus indemnity if wrong.

### C. Disclosure and knowledge (clauses 1.1, 1.2, 8.3; Schedule 7)

- **Clause 1.1 (entire data room disclosed).** This is a general disclosure that deems every document in the data room to be disclosed against every warranty. It effectively eliminates warranty claims for anything the Buyer reviewed. **Strike it.** Disclosure should be specific, identifying the document and the particular fact, and should be fairly disclosed.
- **Clause 1.2 (Accounts, statutory registers, public records).** Same problem. Public records are not disclosure against specific warranties. Strike, or limit to specific references.
- **Clause 8.3 (buyer knowledge).** Bars claims for any matter the Buyer "had knowledge of" or that was "discoverable" in the data room. This is a sandbagging bar. **Strike it and include a pro-sandbagging clause** (the Buyer may claim whether or not it knew of the breach). If the Seller will not accept that, the fallback is that matters specifically disclosed in writing against a specific warranty are excluded, and that known matters are dealt with by specific indemnities. Constructive knowledge ("discoverable") should be deleted in all cases.
- **Interaction with W&I insurance.** If the Buyer is using W&I, insurers will typically exclude known matters. That makes specific indemnities essential, not optional.

### D. Time limits (clauses 12.3, 13)

- General warranties at 18 months are short for a SaaS business with contract-renewal, tax and privacy exposure. Opening ask: **36 months**; fallback **24 months**.
- The Seller's proposal that "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims" must be rejected. Each category needs its own period:
  - Fundamental and title warranties: the longest available (NSW simple contract limitation is generally 6 years under the Limitation Act 1969 (NSW); the parties can vary this by agreement, so the contract should be explicit).
  - Tax: until 60 days after the relevant ATO amendment period expires (generally four years from assessment, subject to exceptions).
  - Specific indemnities (privacy, Ironquay, bonuses, Bluefen): a period matching the exposure (e.g., 24 to 36 months for privacy; until the relevant third-party limitation period expires for IP).

NSW counsel should confirm the limitation position for any clause that purports to shorten the statutory period.

### E. Exclusive remedy, non-reliance and limitations (clauses 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)

- These apply to "all Claims of any nature." **Carve out:** fraud, wilful misconduct, fundamental warranties, tax indemnity, and specific indemnities.
- Non-reliance and exclusion clauses generally cannot protect a party against its own fraud. They also need to be checked against the misleading-conduct provisions of the Australian Consumer Law (s 18), because a non-reliance clause in an SPA may not defeat statutory misleading-conduct claims. NSW counsel should review the final wording.
- Exclusive-remedy language should not stop the Buyer seeking specific performance or injunctive relief (for example, for conditions or completion deliverables).

### F. Title (Schedule 7 item 10; DD-012)

The share register shows Harbourglass as holder of 100%. That is a starting point, not verification. The Buyer should:
- Obtain an ASIC current company extract and a search of the register of members;
- Run PPSR and other encumbrance searches over the shares;
- Require a signed share transfer and register update as a Completion deliverable;
- Get a fundamental warranty that the Seller is the sole legal and beneficial owner, free of encumbrances, with full power to sell.

### G. Tax and IP

The Seller says tax and IP warranties are "settled under the general regime." They are not. Tax needs a standalone pre-Completion tax indemnity, outside the basket and general cap, with the time limit above. IP title warranties (including Ironquay) should be fundamental-level.

### H. Funds flow and price mechanics

- The funds flow excludes the bonuses and does not show the Riverlark payoff. The Seller says it "reflects the agreed price mechanics," but the debt-free/cash-free baseline requires debt to be repaid from the price and a net debt and debt-like items adjustment.
- Opening ask: a completion accounts mechanism (or locked box with leakage protection) that covers net debt, working capital, and debt-like items (bonuses plus on-costs, Riverlark, open Ironquay fees, committed supplier costs, any tax on pre-Completion income).
- Escrow or retention for known and unquantified items (Bluefen, privacy, tax), sized after the investigation outcomes are known.

## Information requests to the Seller

1. Full draft SPA and all schedules (to verify clause references and the general cap/basket/time mechanics).
2. Written record of any principal-level agreement on the "settled" positions.
3. Bluefen change-control consent status, conditions under clause 11.3, and expected timing.
4. Riverlark payoff letter, PPSR schedule, and discharge arrangements.
5. Ironquay: SOW3 invoices, payment history, and the clause 7.3 deliverables; confirm whether any other SOWs are open.
6. Bonus schedule: each employee, amount, conditions, and payroll tax/super calculation.
7. Privacy incident: full forensic report, access logs, the external recipient's identity and handling confirmations, any OAIC/individual notification analysis, and a list of prior incidents.
8. Lease: copy of the lease, the relevant notification and consent clauses, and landlord correspondence.
9. Sandbar renewals: contracts, terms, termination rights, and whether they are required for operations.
10. Mossvale: the relevant assignment clause and the Seller's legal basis for saying it does not apply to a share sale.
11. Confirmation of title: ASIC extract and register of members, plus evidence that no encumbrance exists over shares.

## Summary of recommendations

**Priority 1: Must-have (deal-breakers if refused)**
1. Strike the general disclosure of the data room (1.1) and public records (1.2); disclosure must be specific.
2. Strike the buyer-knowledge bar (8.3) and include pro-sandbagging language.
3. Make Bluefen consent a condition precedent with no "reasonable endeavours" or deemed satisfaction. Add a Bluefen-specific protection if consent is obtained on conditions.
4. Carve title, capacity, fraud and tax out of the general cap, basket, de minimis and time limits.
5. Require Riverlark repayment and security discharge at Completion, paid from the price.
6. Resolve the bonuses (including on-costs) as a debt-like item or Seller-paid liability in the funds flow.

**Priority 2: Strongly recommended**
7. Replace the 20% cap with a 30% opening ask (fallback 20% only with known items carved out); tipping basket at ~0.5% (fallback 1%); de minimis at AUD 10,000.
8. Extend general warranty period to 36 months (fallback 24); fundamental and title to 6 years; tax to ATO period plus 60 days.
9. Specific indemnities (outside the cap) for: Ironquay IP and SOW fees; privacy incident (with investigation completed pre-Completion); Bluefen revenue loss within a defined window; pre-Completion tax.
10. Strike the "any limitation applies to all Claims" language.
11. Limit clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 to exclude fraud, fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities; confirm consistency with ACL.

**Priority 3: Verification and price mechanics**
12. Completion accounts or locked box with leakage, covering net debt, working capital and debt-like items.
13. Title verification (ASIC, register, encumbrance searches) before signing.
14. Lease consent or estoppel and Mossvale confirmation before Completion.
15. Sandbar renewal review, and a covenant on new commitments.
16. Privacy incident investigation and forensic report as a pre-signing or pre-Completion deliverable.

**Process:** Reject the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing unless the Seller produces the signed principal-level terms. Engage NSW counsel on the limitation, non-reliance and ACL points before finalising the mark-up, and get a W&I broker view on what cover is available given the disclosed matters.
=== END ADVICE ===
